slides.heading: Levenshtein Distance
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Medium · Dynamic Programming
slides.narration: Let's solve Levenshtein Distance, a medium dynamic programming problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Minimum single-char inserts/deletes/substitutions turning a into b.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Minimum single-char inserts or deletes or substitutions turning a into b.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Dynamic programming over prefixes: each cell is the cheapest edit between two prefixes.
slides.narration: Dynamic programming over prefixes: each cell is the cheapest edit between two prefixes.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: recursively try insert/delete/replace → O(3^(n+m))
DP table over prefixes → O(n·m) time
Keep only two rows → O(min(n, m)) space
slides.narration: Recursively trying every edit branches three ways at each step, which is exponential. The same subproblems repeat, so a table over prefixes solves it in n times m. Since each row only needs the previous one, two rows suffice.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Row zero and column zero are insert or delete costs
3. Otherwise one plus the min of insert, delete, replace
slides.narration: Step by step. First, row zero and column zero are insert or delete costs. Second, equal characters copy the diagonal. Third, otherwise one plus the min of insert, delete, replace. Fourth, two rows suffice.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Base row/column: edits from/to the empty string
slides.narration: The first row and column are the cost of building a prefix from nothing: just insertions or deletions.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 'a' → 'ya': 'a' = 'a' → copy diagonal 1
slides.narration: Turning a into ya: the last letters are both a, so the cost equals the diagonal, 1.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 'ab' → 'yab': 'b' = 'b' → copy diagonal 1
slides.narration: Turning ab into yab: the last letters are both b, so the cost equals the diagonal, 1.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 'abc' → 'yab': 1 + min(neighbours) = 2
slides.narration: Turning abc into yab: the last letters differ, so we pay one plus the cheapest of replace, delete or insert: 2.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 'abc' → 'yabd': 1 + min(neighbours) = 2
slides.narration: Turning abc into yabd: the last letters differ, so we pay one plus the cheapest of replace, delete or insert: 2.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We swap so b is the shorter string, initialise the previous row to zero through m, and for each character of a fill the current row: equal characters copy the diagonal, otherwise one plus the min of the three neighbours. Then we swap rows and return the last value.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n times m. Space is O of min(n, m).

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Swap so the shorter string defines the row length
slides.narration: If either string is empty, the answer is the other's length. The table has one extra row and column for the empty prefix, a common off-by-one trap.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Explain the three neighbours: replace, delete, insert
Follow-up: reconstruct the edits; weighted costs
slides.narration: Name the three neighbours explicitly: diagonal is replace, above is delete, left is insert. Follow-ups reconstruct the edit script or use weighted costs.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Dynamic programming over prefixes: each cell is the cheapest edit between two prefixes.
slides.narration: To recap Levenshtein Distance: Dynamic programming over prefixes: each cell is the cheapest edit between two prefixes. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
